tip: Body states use 'estar com' plus a noun: 'estou com calor' is literally "I'm with heat". Spanish reaches for 'tengo', French for 'j'ai', but Portuguese picks 'estar com'.
'Não tem de quê' is a set reply to 'obrigado' (thanks). The words are fixed, so you do not change them.
In Portuguese, you "are with hunger" ('estar com fome'), not "have hunger". Same pattern: 'estar com sede' (thirsty), 'estar com frio' (cold).
To say how many are in a group, use 'ser' plus a number: 'somos cinco' = there are five of us.
'Tenho muito sono' is literally "I have much sleep". Portuguese uses 'ter' (to have) where English uses "to be" for this state.
'Morar' = to live (reside). 'Viver' = to live (be alive). Portuguese normally keeps these separate: 'moram juntos' = they live together.
'Têm' with a circumflex is the 'vocês'/'eles' form of 'ter'. The singular 'tem' has no accent.
'Tudo bom' is a casual greeting, like "how are you". You can also answer with 'tudo bom'.
'Cozinha' does double duty: it is both "she cooks", the verb, and "the kitchen", the noun. Context tells you which.
'Muito' before an adjective/adverb = very. Before a noun = much/many: 'muito dinheiro'.
'Elas' is "they" for an all-female group. Use 'eles' if even one man is included.
In Portuguese, you "have" years, not "are" years old: 'tem trinta anos' = is thirty years old.
The circumflex marks number: 'têm' is the 'eles'/'elas' form, 'tem' the 'ele'/'ela' form. 'Eles têm três filhos' needs the accent.
'Ir embora' means to leave/go away. 'Embora' adds the sense of departure that plain 'ir' doesn't have. 'Vou embora' = I'm leaving.
'Descansa' is the casual command. In everyday speech the command usually just matches the 'ele' present form: 'descansa'.
'Pela' is 'por' plus 'a', meaning through or via: 'pela internet' = online.
'Dele' = his ('de' + 'ele'). 'Dela' = hers ('de' + 'ela'). These are used far more than 'seu'/'sua' to avoid ambiguity in Brazilian Portuguese.
'Estar' covers how you are right now: 'está ocupado' means busy at the moment, not that he is a busy sort of person.
'Ô de casa' is a traditional way to announce yourself at someone's door.
'Todo' directly before a singular noun (no article) means "every": 'todo dia' = every day, 'todo mês' = every month.
'Estou com saudade' is how you say you miss someone: 'saudade', like 'fome' or 'frio', normally takes 'estar com' rather than a direct verb.
'Gostar' always needs 'de' before its object: 'gosta de cozinhar'. English "like" takes no preposition, but dropping 'de' here breaks the sentence.
'Daqui' is the contraction of 'de + aqui' (from here). These contractions are mandatory in Portuguese.
'Algum' means any or some and agrees with its noun: 'algum esporte', 'alguma ideia'.
'Precisar' plus an infinitive normally takes no preposition: 'preciso trocar'. Before a noun you add 'de'.
'Do' is the contraction of 'de' plus 'o', so 'longe do trabalho' means far from work.
In Brazilian Portuguese, 'assistir' takes a direct object without 'a': 'assiste futebol', not 'assiste ao futebol' (the 'a' survives in formal writing).
'Vocês' is the everyday "you all" across Brazil; the older 'tu' forms survive only in some regions.
Present tense is often used for scheduled future events in Portuguese: 'assino amanhã' = I'll sign tomorrow.
'Próprio' agrees with its noun for "own": 'próprias roupas' (feminine plural). Masculine would be 'próprios'.
